title: Pinet: Optimizing hard-constrained neural networks with orthogonal projection layers
claim: A differentiable projection layer maps infeasible network outputs onto the feasible set, with gradients flowing back through it to the backbone.
layout: 3 colored panels, left-to-right, curved backprop arrows running right-to-left
description: Three rounded, pastel-tinted panels run left to right. The blue panel shows a small fully connected backbone network with input x and an output layer. Wavy dashed blue lines connect its outputs to a point f(x) in the pink panel, which shows 3D axes and a red polyhedron as the feasible set. An orange arrow projects the blue infeasible point f(x) onto the polytope, giving the orange point y. The cream panel on the right shows 2D axes, a red pentagon, and concentric contour lines for the loss φ(y,x), with the orange point y inside the pentagon. Black curved arrows labeled Backprop point right to left between the panels. A GitHub link and a pip install line sit along the top. Panel labels are at the bottom of each panel.
caption: Illustration of the \ouralg architecture. The infeasible output of the backbone network is projected onto the feasible set through an operator splitting scheme. To train the backbone network, we use the implicit function theorem to backpropagate the loss through the projection layer.
abstract: We introduce an output layer for neural networks that ensures satisfaction of convex constraints. Our approach, $Î $net, leverages operator splitting for rapid and reliable projections in the forward pass, and the implicit function theorem for backpropagation. We deploy $Î $net as a feasible-by-design optimization proxy for parametric constrained optimization problems and obtain modest-accuracy solutions faster than traditional solvers when solving a single problem, and significantly faster for a batch of problems. We surpass state-of-the-art learning approaches by orders of magnitude in terms of training time, solution quality, and robustness to hyperparameter tuning, while maintaining similar inference times. Finally, we tackle multi-vehicle motion planning with non-convex trajectory preferences and provide $Î $net as a GPU-ready package implemented in JAX.
